judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: Link in the article's Language panel whose text is the Hebrew name of the language. The snapshot and the live HTML (fetched 2026-10-28) show 🇮🇱 עברית with no lang on the link, the span or any ancestor, and html lang="en". The panel is visually closed in the screenshot but stays in the accessibility tree (not aria-hidden), so screen readers reach it, and it shows when opened. I looked for reasons it might pass: language names are not proper names or vernacular words in English, and the Understanding document for 3.1.2 gives this case (alternative language links, each language name written in that language and marked with lang) as its example. A screen reader guessing the language from the script is not a WCAG technique. Real 3.1.2 failure.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: Visible newsletter sign-up field ('Enter your email') that asks for the user's own email address. Snapshot and live HTML: <input type="email" placeholder="Enter your email"> with no autocomplete attribute. The email purpose is in the Input Purposes list and HTML can identify it, so 1.3.5 applies. I checked whether anything else makes it pass: type="email" only sets the data format, not the autocomplete purpose that H98 relies on, and no autocomplete is added at runtime in the snapshot. Real 1.3.5 failure. The field also has only a placeholder as its label, which concerns other criteria.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: The h3 'Mr Alex Day' is the title of an image card in the article. The screenshot shows a bordered box with 'Mr Alex Day' above a photo of him (alt 'Mr Alex Day, Consultant Ophthalmologist...') and a 'View larger' button. The heading names exactly what the card holds, and the paragraphs around it quote Day's advice, so it describes its topic. Using a heading as an image caption might be argued under 1.3.1, but it is not a 2.4.6 failure. The model misjudged content it had.

judgments.label: false_positive
judgments.rationale: Inline link in article prose: 'we've followed the tradition of setting off fireworks', pointing to 'Managing PTSD during fireworks season'. 2.4.4 asks that the link's purpose be determinable from its text and its programmatically determined context (the sentence). It does not ask that link text match the destination's title. The link is a topical cross-reference to a related fireworks article. Any loss of clarity applies equally to sighted readers, and that case falls under the criterion's 'ambiguous to users in general' exception. No documented 2.4.4 failure covers loose editorial link wording. The finding applies a stricter text-matches-destination rule than WCAG's.
